::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Find the tangent between two points](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4680500/find-the-tangent-between-two-points), asked by [Need_MathHelp](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1135253/need-mathhelp) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-04-16; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Let $f(x) = x^3$. Show that for every point $P = (x_0, y_0) \in\mathbb R^2$ there is a tangent to the graph of $f(x)$ that passes through $P$.
>
> I said in order for this to be true $f'(x)$ needs to be defined for all $f(x)$ and for all $x$'s. If this is true then we will have a value for all $f'(x)$. This means that $f(x)$ will be able to give us all types of straight lines that both grows and decreases. So I differentiated $f(x)$ to $3x^2$ and here we can see that $f'(x)$ is defined for all x's and thus there is a line for every $(x_0, y_0)$ that passes through the point $p$. 
>
> But in the answers they used mean value theorem etc, but I was wondering if my explanation was totally wrong because I got $0$ point on it.
:::

Your explanation is intuitive, and could be plausible with accompanying illustrations, but it isn't rigorous or convincing. If one of my students had answered that question that way, I would have given some credit for understanding the statement.

Every point on the graph of $f(x) = x^3$ will already have a tangent line through it, because the function is differentiable. If $P = (x_0,y_0)$ is *not* on the the graph, and $(x,x^3)$ *is* on the graph, then the line between them has slope $\frac{x^3-y_0}{x-x_0}$. That line is tangent to the graph of $f$ if the slope equals $f'(x) = 3x^2$.

So you are looking for a real number $x$ such that
$$\frac{x^3-y_0}{x-x_0} = 3x^2 \iff x^3 - y_0 = 3x^2(x-x_0)
    \iff 2x^3 - 3x^2 x_0 + y_0 = 0$$
Every cubic polynomial has a real root, so we know some $x$ satisfies the equation.
